All Managers / Functional Leaders must:

Instil a zero-tolerance approach to fraud, bribery, and corruption in their teams.

Ensure they understand how fraud, bribery and corruption risk may happen in their area.

Assess fraud risks in the areas they are responsible for, in conjunction with the Enterprise Risk team, using Fraud Impact Assessments.

Ensure that fraud, bribery, corruption, and unethical behaviour controls in their areas are operating effectively, and the controls are regularly tested and reviewed.

Attend relevant training and awareness activities in order that they can detect fraud.

Ensure that their teams participate in fraud, bribery, and corruption training to help them recognise and understand these risks.

Ensure staff are supported in raising any concerns of fraud, bribery, and corruption.

Satisfy themselves that travel and expense claims, timesheets, and entries into the gifts and hospitality register are valid and accurate before approving.

Work with the relevant Risk Partner to undertake Initial Fraud Impact Assessments (IFIA) and Fraud Risk Assessments (FRA) for all areas of spend for which the business case will require approval outside of NWS delegation.

All Staff must:

Act with integrity and honesty at all times.

Never offer or accept a bribe or participate in any fraud, bribery, corruption, or unethical behaviour with their work at NWS.

Act with propriety in the handling of public funds, resources, assets, and information.

Be alert to the possibility of fraud, bribery, corruption and any behaviours or indicators of such.

Understand they have a part to play in protecting NWS from fraud, bribery, corruption, and unethical behaviour, and comply with NWS processes and controls designed to mitigate these risks.

Complete expense claims, timesheets, and gifts and hospitality registers honestly and in line with the relevant policies and procedures.

Undertake counter fraud, bribery, and corruption training appropriate to their role, when required.

Notify any concerns of fraud, bribery, corruption, and unethical behaviour (which may be red flags or unusual events) in line with the Fraud, Bribery and Corruption Response Plan.

4. Suspected Fraud, Bribery & Corruption

How suspected fraud, bribery and corruption may be discovered.

Suspected fraud, bribery, and corruption may come to light through a variety of means, which may include: - • routine processes/system checks.

proactive detection mechanisms, such as data analytics.

management follow up on areas where there is evidence that controls are not being applied.

auditor or assurance reviews.

concerns having been raised to a Line Manager, or to the Head of Enterprise Risk and Assurance and / or the General Counsel/Company Secretary or a report through the NDA Group’s independent whistleblowing hotline, Safecall; or

other ‘tip offs’ from members of staff or third parties.

How to report suspicions of fraud, bribery, and corruption All employees are responsible for notifying suspected fraud, bribery, and corruption that they become aware of. Any suspected or potential fraud, bribery or corruption should be reported through one (or more) of the following methods, as per the NWS Speak Up Policy and Guidance document.

Line Manager Where appropriate, suspicions and allegations can be raised with an employee’s line manager. Where appropriate, managers must support employees in raising their concerns in line with the Fraud, Bribery and Corruption Policy and the Response Plan.

Head of Enterprise Risk and Assurance or General Counsel/Company Secretary Employees may also contact the Head of Enterprise Risk and Assurance and / or the General Counsel/Company Secretary with any allegations or suspicions.

Safecall Our confidential whistleblowing reporting service (www.safecall.co.uk / 0800 915 1571) is available for any concern where it is considered that any of the internal methods above is inappropriate, for whatever reason. Any complaints alleging wrongdoing in our workplaces are received by Accountable Senior Officer for Fraud, Bribery, and Corruption (the General Counsel/Company Secretary) will progress the initial response independently and with complete impartiality.

Within the NDA Group If you feel you cannot speak up within NWS, you may do so to via the NDA Ethics & Compliance Team eandc@nda.gov.uk or use Safecall and indicate you wish the concern to be raised as an NDA matter. They will then oversee the resolution of your matter, involving NWS as appropriate.

Reporting other concerns Health, safety and security observations, incidents and allegations should be reported through our dedicated system, OSHENS.

Cyber security concerns, breaches, or incidents should be reported to the Information Security team as soon as possible, using their Reporting Form.

5. Sanctions and Redress

In cases of serious fraud and/or bribery, NWS reserve the right to apply sanctions. These may include;

Disciplinary action in line with the NWS Disciplinary Policy.

Civil action to recover lost funds.

Use of criminal law to apply an appropriate criminal penalty upon the individual(s).

Referral of information and evidence to external bodies, e.g. professional bodies, if appropriate.

Disciplinary procedures in line with the NWS Disciplinary Policy will be initiated where an employee is suspected of being involved in a fraudulent or illegal act. The Accountable Senior Officer, in conjunction with the HR Department, will be responsible for initiating any necessary disciplinary action.

Effective from 1 September 2025, the offence of Failure to prevent Fraud also holds organisations to account should they profit from fraud committed by their employees. Under the new offence, NWS will be liable where a specified fraud offence is committed by an employee or agent, for the organisation’s benefit, where we did not have reasonable fraud prevention procedures in place. It does not need to be demonstrated that management or the Board either ordered or knew about the fraud, and prosecution may result in an unlimited fine to the organisation, or to specific employees.

Bribery is the offering, promising, or giving of a financial or other advantage to induce or reward improper performance and/or the request for, or acceptance of such an advantage.

The Bribery Act 2010 sets out four offences:

Offering a bribe - offering, promising, or giving of a financial reward or other inducement or advantage to another person to perform a relevant function or activity improperly.

Accepting a bribe - requesting, agreeing to receive, or accepting a financial reward or other inducement or advantage to perform a function or activity improperly, directly, or indirectly, and irrespective of whether it is for the recipient’s benefit.

Bribing a foreign public official – offering or giving a financial (or other) advantage or inducement to a foreign public official, with the intention of influencing that public official in the carrying out of their duties. Any intent to influence is sufficient – it does not have to be an intent to influence the public official to carry out their duties improperly. The definition of foreign public official may be widely interpreted (for example it may include university employees in some countries).

Failure of a commercial organisation to prevent bribery – NWS is responsible for acts of bribery carried out by “associated” persons for our benefit. Associated parties may include those who carry out services for or on our behalf such as agents or intermediaries. An organisation can commit an offence under Section 7 of the Bribery Act 2010, which is failing to prevent a bribe, if an employee, subsidiary, or associated person commits bribery within it. The organisation has a defence against this offence if it can demonstrate it has adequate anti-bribery controls and procedures in place.

Inducements or advantages may include, but are not limited to, gifts; favourable commercial arrangements; hospitality, such as meals, hotel stays, tickets, or invitations to sporting or cultural events; favours that are of value to the recipient (such as offers of employment, work experience or internships); and charitable donations.

These items are not always bribes, but because of the risk that they are bribes or may be perceived as bribes, we have processes and controls in place (such as gifts and hospitality registers) to manage this risk which everyone must comply with.

Facilitation payments (sometimes known as grease payments), whereby unofficial payments or gifts are made to secure, facilitate or speed-up a public official’s performance of a necessary government action or process are bribes (even if they are of low value) and should not be made.

There is a defence to the corporate offence if NWS can show we had “adequate procedures” in place designed to prevent bribery. Guidance issued by the Ministry of Justice sets out six broad management principles to assist organisations to put in place proper anti-bribery procedures. NWS will follow these principles to show that it is committed to eliminating bribery within or on behalf of the business.

The management principles are:

Proportionality – anti-bribery policies and procedures should be proportionate to the activities and size of the organisation, the sector in which it operates and the risks it faces.

Top level commitment – establishing a clear culture within the Organisation which reinforces that bribery is unacceptable.

Risk assessment – understanding and keeping up to date with the bribery risks it faces by carrying out regular risk assessments using Fraud Impact Assessment tools.

Due diligence – the Organisation needs to know details about who it does business with, who it is paying money to and why – and make sure those the organisation works with, e.g. associated persons, also have reciprocal anti-bribery agreements in place.

Corruption is the deliberate abuse of a public or private office for personal gain. This can take many forms, such as fraud, extortion, cronyism, bribery, or facilitation payments.

Theft

Theft is broadly included in the definition of fraud. The three main offences in the Theft Act 1968 are:

Section 1: Theft - dishonestly taking property of another with the intention of permanently depriving the owner of it for example taking company property off the premises without a legitimate reason.

Section 17: False Accounting - dishonestly destroys, conceals, or falsifies any accounting record or produces a misleading accounting record with a view to reporting misleading financial performance - for example exaggerating financial performance.

Section 24a: Retaining Wrongful Credit - dishonestly fails to take reasonable steps to ensure that a wrongful credit is cancelled for example taking no action to cancel incorrect salary enhancements received.

Facilitating Tax Evasion means being knowingly concerned in, or taking steps with a view to, the tax evasion of another, and/or aiding and abetting another person’s offence of tax evasion. An example of this is helping another person to evade tax by deliberately wrongly completing the tool used to assess whether an individual is inside or outside IR35 rules.
